what_its_for: This medication is used to lower the pressure inside your eye. It is used to treat open-angle glaucoma or a condition called ocular hypertension (high eye pressure). Controlling eye pressure helps protect your vision and prevent damage to the optic nerve.
how_to_take: This medication is NOT something you take by mouth or put in your eye yourself. It is a tiny implant that your eye doctor (ophthalmologist) places inside your eye during a short in-office procedure. The implant slowly releases medicine into your eye over time. You do not need to do anything special to use it after it is placed — the implant works automatically.
dosing: Your doctor will place one implant in each affected eye during a single office visit procedure. The implant continuously releases a small amount of travoprost into your eye every day. You do not need to remember to use eye drops daily — the implant does this work for you automatically. The implant is designed to last for a long period of time (approximately 3 years or as directed by your doctor). Your doctor will monitor the implant and replace it if needed.
missed_dose: Because this is an implant placed by your doctor, there are no doses for you to remember or miss. The implant delivers medicine automatically. However, it is very important that you keep all scheduled follow-up appointments with your eye doctor so they can check that the implant is working properly and your eye pressure is under control.
storage: You do not need to store this medication at home. The implant is kept and managed by your eye doctor's office. After the implant is placed in your eye, no special storage steps are needed on your part.
what_to_avoid:
- Do not rub or press hard on your eye after the implant procedure, as this could cause irritation or affect the implant.
- Avoid swimming or submerging your head in water (pools, hot tubs) for the time period your doctor recommends after the procedure.
- Avoid wearing contact lenses until your doctor says it is safe to do so after the procedure.
- Tell all of your doctors and your pharmacist about this implant, since some eye medications or procedures could interfere with it.
- Do not use any other eye drops or medications in the treated eye unless your eye doctor specifically tells you to.
when_to_call_doctor:
Contact your eye doctor right away if you notice any of the following:
- Sudden changes in your vision or blurred vision
- Eye pain, redness, or increased sensitivity to light
- Feeling like something is in your eye
- Eye discharge or unusual tearing
- Swelling around your eye
- The implant appears to have moved or you can see it in a different position
- Any signs of eye infection such as increased redness, discharge, or worsening pain
- Headache or nausea that you think may be related to your eye
If you experience sudden vision loss, go to an emergency room immediately.
when_it_works: The implant begins releasing medicine right after it is placed in your eye. Your eye doctor will check your eye pressure at follow-up visits to confirm the implant is working. Most patients begin to see a reduction in eye pressure within the first few weeks after placement. It is important to attend all follow-up appointments so your doctor can make sure the medication is controlling your eye pressure effectively.
special_populations:
- Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of this implant during pregnancy or breastfeeding has not been fully established, and your doctor will help weigh the risks and benefits.
- Children: This implant is generally intended for use in adults. Talk to your doctor if you have questions about use in younger patients.
- Older Adults: No special adjustments are typically needed for older adults, but regular follow-up visits remain very important.
- Patients with other eye conditions: Tell your doctor about any other eye problems, previous eye surgeries, or eye infections you have had, as these may affect whether this implant is right for you.
